fields.Front: Which internally driven processes does Unit 2 exclude and why?
fields.Back: Landslides, land subsidence etc. - too small to ever make it onto the catastrophic events scale.

fields.Front: List Earth's layers by chemical composition (older terminology).
fields.Back: Crust (thin outer shell), mantle (dense silicate and oxide minerals), core (metallic: liquid outer core, solid inner core), topped by oceans and atmosphere.

fields.Front: List Earth's layers by physical properties (newer terminology), surface to centre.
fields.Back: Lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core, inner core.

fields.Text: Physical layers of Earth, surface to centre: {{c1::lithosphere}}, {{c2::asthenosphere}}, {{c3::mesosphere}}, outer core, inner core.
The inner core is {{c1::solid}} iron-nickel metal at an estimated {{c2::5000-7000 C}} (Ch. 3), spinning at least {{c3::0.2 degrees}} of longitude per year faster than Earth.
fields.Extra: Hot, solid, nearly pure metal (mostly iron and nickel); Chapter 3 estimates 5000-7000 C, spinning at least 0.2 degrees of longitude per year faster than Earth.

fields.Text: The outer core is {{c1::liquid}} iron-nickel metal whose circulating currents generate Earth's {{c2::magnetic field}} (dynamo model).
fields.Extra: Similarly hot but liquid metal (molten iron and nickel); its circulating currents generate the magnetic field (dynamo).

fields.Text: The {{c1::mesosphere}} is the lower, thick zone of the mantle: very dense rock that behaves as a {{c2::solid}} ('stiff plastic').
fields.Extra: The lower, thick zone of the mantle: very dense rock that behaves as a solid ('stiff plastic').

fields.Front: Define the asthenosphere.
fields.Back: A thin zone of the upper mantle, same composition as the mesosphere but under much less confining pressure, so it behaves like a hot plastic and may locally be fluid.

fields.Front: Define the lithosphere.
fields.Back: The crust plus the really thin, cold, brittle top layer of the mantle that is 'stuck' to the crust - Earth's rigid outer shell.

fields.Text: The lithosphere = the {{c1::crust}} plus the cold, brittle uppermost {{c2::mantle}}; beneath it the {{c3::asthenosphere}} behaves like a hot plastic.

fields.Front: Why does the asthenosphere behave differently from the mesosphere despite the same composition?
fields.Back: It is nearer the top of the mantle and under much less confining pressure.

fields.Front: Two types of crust?
fields.Back: Oceanic and continental.

fields.Front: Approximate depths (Fig. 2): base of lithosphere, base of asthenosphere, base of mantle, base of outer core, centre?
Approximate densities (Fig. 2): ocean water, continental crust, upper mantle, inner core?
fields.Back: 1.03, 2.7, 3.3 g/cm3 (mantle rises to 5.7 at its base); core 9.7-16 g/cm3.

fields.Text: {{c1::Differentiation}} is the gravity-driven movement of {{c2::heavy}} material to the core and {{c3::lighter}} material outward, once Earth was hot enough to flow.
fields.Extra: The process, once Earth was hot and liquid enough for material to move freely, of heavy material sinking (by gravity) to the core and lighter material moving outward, producing the layered structure.

fields.Text: {{c1::Accretion}} is the growth of a body as smaller objects stick to it; Earth began by accretion of {{c2::cold}} material.
fields.Extra: The growth of a body as smaller objects (asteroids, meteoroids, dust) stick to it; Earth began by accretion of cold material.

fields.Text: Earth's interior may reach {{c1::7200-7500 C}}, more than {{c2::1000 C}} hotter than the Sun's outer layer.
fields.Extra: As high as 7200-7500 C - more than 1000 C higher than the Sun's outer layer.

fields.Front: Name the four mechanisms by which Earth was/is heated.
fields.Back: 1) Accretion and impact heating; 2) core-formation heat; 3) heat from dissipation of tidal energy; 4) heat from radioactivity.

fields.Text: Earth's four heat sources: {{c1::accretion/impact heating}}, {{c2::core formation}} (gravitational potential energy), {{c3::tidal dissipation}}, and radioactivity.

fields.Front: Which heat source was most important in early Earth formation, and which is most important now?
fields.Back: Early: accretion/impact heating (kinetic energy; plus core formation and short-lived isotopes). Now: radioactivity (long-lived K, U, Th) - virtually all current internal energy.

fields.Front: Define kinetic energy and give its formula.
fields.Back: The energy possessed by a body because of its motion: KE = 1/2 m v^2 (m = mass, v = velocity). 'Remember this equation!'

fields.Text: Kinetic Energy = {{c1::1/2 m v^2}}, where m is mass and v is velocity.
A 1979 calculation showed early impacts would heat a body of {{c1::1000 km}} radius by {{c2::1000 C}} - enough to melt early Earth completely.
fields.Extra: For a body of 1000 km radius, energy from early Solar System impacts would raise its temperature by 1000 C - so early Earth would have melted completely from impact heat alone.

fields.Front: How did the Moon form?
fields.Back: From debris when the Mars-sized planet Theia side-swiped Earth early in Solar System history; the impact's kinetic energy helped melt and differentiate Earth.

fields.Front: What energy is released during core formation?
fields.Back: Gravitational potential energy, as dense material segregates to the core ('drop a book on your toes').

fields.Front: How long did core formation take, and what is this phase called?
fields.Back: No more than a couple of million years; 'the iron catastrophe'.

fields.Text: Core formation released {{c1::gravitational potential}} energy, took no more than {{c2::a couple of million}} years, and is called the {{c3::iron catastrophe}}.

fields.Front: Where is tidal heating especially important?
fields.Back: In small satellites (moons) whose content of radioactive isotopes may be small.

fields.Text: The highest tide in Earth's asthenosphere/mantle is only {{c1::11 cm}}, so it is hard to detect.
Tidal braking has {{c1::slowed Earth's rotation}} and made the Moon slowly {{c2::recede}}; the braking energy is manifested as {{c3::heat}}.
fields.Extra: Slowed Earth's rotation rate and caused the Moon to slowly recede; the energy of braking Earth's rotation becomes heat (tidal braking).

fields.Front: What do decaying isotopes release?
fields.Back: They may release particles (electrons, alpha particles) and always release energy (gamma rays, X-rays).

fields.Front: Two categories of radioactivity relevant to Earth's heat?
fields.Back: Long-lived radioactivity (K, U, Th) and short-lived radioactivity (e.g. 26Al), the latter now virtually gone.

fields.Front: Give the example of a short-lived radioactive isotope: parent, daughter, half-life, status.
fields.Back: Aluminum-26 -> magnesium-26; half-life 720,000 years; essentially extinct now, but once a major heat source because Al is abundant.

fields.Text: {{c1::Aluminum-26}} decays to magnesium-26 with a half-life of {{c2::720,000}} years and is now essentially extinct.
Long-lived radioactive isotopes of {{c1::potassium (K)}}, {{c2::uranium (U)}} and {{c3::thorium (Th)}} supply virtually all of Earth's internal heat today.
fields.Extra: Isotopes of potassium (K), uranium (U) and thorium (Th).

fields.Front: Define heat flow.
fields.Back: Heat escaping per unit time from Earth's interior across each unit of surface area; measured on all continents and oceans.

fields.Front: Why has heat flow decreased over Earth's history?
fields.Back: Solid crust and oceans formed and act as insulation between the hot mantle and atmosphere; short-lived isotopes declined; only long-lived radioactivity remains. Change is slight over any long period.

fields.Front: Will Earth's internal heat run out?
fields.Back: Eventually, as long-lived radioactive isotopes decrease in abundance - but no detectable change is expected any time soon.

fields.Front: What are 'plates' and 'tectonics'?
fields.Back: Plates: large segments of Earth's crust/lithosphere. Tectonics: the processes by which plates interact along their boundaries in response to escaping internal heat.

fields.Front: How are the edges of tectonic plates defined?
fields.Back: By the traces (lines) of earthquakes and volcanoes, concentrated along subduction zones and transform faults.
